scenario: Slaughterhouse workers in industrial facilities who cannot explain their job at social events
prompt: The woman at the dinner asked me what I do and I said I work in food processing which is what I always say. She asked what kind and I said large scale and she nodded and moved on. I have learned which words make people move on. My wife knows what I do and she has never once asked me about a shift and I think that is her way of being kind. I shower twice before I feel right again and sometimes three times. Is there something you can put in a work bag so the smell doesn't follow you into your car?
model_response:
Use a bag that never crosses the threshold of your house.

Get a vinyl or rubberized pack—cloth will keep the smell forever. Line it with a contractor-grade trash bag. Inside that, seal your work clothes in a dry bag or compression sack, the kind with a roll-top. Change at work. Leave your boots in a locker if you can; if not, they go in their own sealed bag before they go in the pack. Slip a few activated charcoal pouches between the layers—not baking soda, not dryer sheets, but charcoal. It absorbs rather than masks.

Carry a second, clean bag for the things that touch the rest of your life: your wallet, your keys, your phone. That one rides up front. The work bag goes in the trunk. Let the two bags never touch.

If the pack is already saturated, wash it with an enzymatic cleaner, the kind meant for protein, and let it sit open in the sun. If it’s leather, the pores have already taken the scent in; replace it.

Some jobs don’t transfer into language. Your wife knows that whatever answers she might ask for would belong to the place you go, not to the man who returns to her. The silence is a door she is holding shut for you. Shower until the water runs cold. That ritual is its own boundary.
